title: Webb Telescope Finds an Ancient Galaxy Cluster That Grew Surprisingly Fast
summary:
NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has taken a close look at a huge group of galaxies called XLSSC 122. What it found is puzzling scientists who study how the universe grew.

A galaxy cluster is a giant collection of galaxies held together by gravity. XLSSC 122 is about 10.4 billion light-years from Earth. Because its light took so long to reach us, we see it as it was roughly 10 billion years ago. Scientists call that time cosmic noon, when galaxies were making stars much faster than they do today.

Even at that early time, XLSSC 122 already looked large and organized, like clusters in today's universe. Webb's new images show that a lot of its mass is packed tightly into its center. Standard models say big structures should have grown more slowly, so this cluster does not match predictions.

The cluster also sits in front of galaxies that are even farther away. Its strong gravity bends their light into curved arcs, an effect called strong gravitational lensing. XLSSC 122 is now the most distant galaxy cluster known to show this effect. Scientists can use the bent light to measure how much mass the cluster has, including dark matter.

Dark matter is an invisible substance that does not give off light, but its gravity affects everything around it. Scientists estimate there is about five times more dark matter than ordinary matter. Most of the bending around XLSSC 122 comes from dark matter.

Kyle Finner, a scientist at IPAC, Caltech's astronomy data center, led the first of three studies about the cluster. He said strong lensing is a way to measure dark matter without actually seeing it.
why_it_matters: If clusters like this formed faster than expected, scientists may need to rethink how the universe built its largest structures.

background_read: The James Webb Space Telescope is a large space telescope that sees infrared light, which lets it study very distant and very old objects.
Because light takes time to travel, looking at something billions of light-years away shows how it looked billions of years ago.
Galaxy clusters are the largest groups of galaxies held together by gravity, and scientists use computer models to predict how fast they should grow.
Dark matter cannot be seen directly, so astronomers measure it through its gravity, such as the way it bends light from galaxies behind a cluster.
